Principles

8 Rules of a Hanseatic Merchant

How German traders ran the Baltic without a state
history uncle co.Swipe
I
Simplified

Trade Through Networks, Not Firms

Hanseatic merchants rarely built large permanent companies. They worked through short partnerships with kin and trusted peers in other towns. Ulf Christian Ewert and Stephan Selzer describe the Hansa as a network organisation rather than a firm.

Ewert and Selzer
history uncle co.historyuncle.substack.com
II

Do Favours, Expect Them Back

A merchant in Lübeck sold goods for a partner in Bruges, who did the same for him, often without a fee. This reciprocal trade kept costs low and bound reputations together. Philippe Dollinger describes it in The German Hansa.

Dollinger 1964

Jacopo Negretti, called Palma Giovane, Portrait of a Gentleman, c. 1590
III

Write Letters, Watch Your Credit

Hildebrand Veckinchusen ran trade from Livonia to Bruges by letter. Wilhelm Stieda edited the correspondence in 1921. Overextended credit and a failed Venice venture ended with him imprisoned for debt in Bruges in the 1420s.

Stieda 1921
history uncle co.historyuncle.substack.com
IV

Obey the Kontor Statute

At the Peterhof in Novgorod, German merchants lived under a written statute, the Skra, revised over generations. It regulated lodging, conduct, the church of St Peter that stored their goods, and the election of aldermen.

Dollinger 1964
history uncle co.historyuncle.substack.com
Claude Monet, Sandvika, Norway, 1895
V

Stay Unmarried at Bergen

At the Bergen Kontor on Bryggen, resident merchants and apprentices were expected to remain unmarried and live inside the wharf compounds. The rule kept the community disciplined, transient and separate from Norwegian society, as Dollinger notes.

Dollinger 1964
history uncle co.historyuncle.substack.com
VI

Know Whose Law Applies

Many Baltic towns adopted the law of Lübeck, and disputes could be referred to Lübeck's council as a higher court. A merchant moving between Reval, Rostock and Wismar met familiar legal rules.

Dollinger 1964
history uncle co.historyuncle.substack.com
VII

Leave When Privileges Fail

In 1358 the Hanseatic towns embargoed Flanders and moved their Bruges Kontor to Dordrecht. By 1360 Flanders had confirmed their privileges and the merchants returned. Collective withdrawal was the Hansa's strongest weapon.

Dollinger 1964
history uncle co.historyuncle.substack.com
VIII
Contested

Keep Your Books Simple

Hanseatic merchants mostly kept single-entry notebooks of debts and shipments, not Italian double entry. Older scholarship read this as backwardness. Many recent historians argue it suited small partnerships built on trust. The point remains contested.

Dollinger 1964
